messages.body_plain:
Dear Andy and all developers of unmarked,

thank you for this great package! I started to use gdistsamp() but I noticed there are
problems with convergence, and it is recommended to provide starting values
using the `starts` argument. Is there any documentation or description of
the format of the `starts` argument? I.e. which parameters in which order and
which format. It will probably depend on the mixture and keyfun settings and
number of covariates as well (I normally use "P" and "halfnorm", but general description
would be welcome).
I could try to hack the source code but I feel safer asking.

Thanks and best regards!

        Tomas

messages.subject: combining predict and ranef to estimate density
messages.subject_clean: combining predict and ranef to estimate density
messages.body_plain:
Hello Unmarked Users,

I would like to estimate density of several species of forest songbirds in twelve ~50 ha forest stands, each of which contain at least ten point count stations.  I have 5 yrs. of post-treatment data and two surveys per year.  I have stacked data so that there are 126 stations x 5 yrs = 630 total rows of data.  I used Year as a covariate in all models.  Each stand has an additional 20 or so plots where we sampled habitat characteristics, but not birds.

So to estimate abundance I used the best gmultmix model for a species, and used "ranef" for plots we surveyed for both birds and habitat and "predict" for plots where we have only habitat data.  Dorazio et al. (2013) did something like this, though I'm not sure if I'm actually duplicating their procedure.  Also Kery et al. (2005) and Royle (2004) both used or advocated Laird & Louis's (1987) empirical Bayes confidence intervals based on bootstrap samples.  I think this is what function Ranef does, but I'm not sure.  I don't understand this function very well and I'm not sure if I'm interpreting these sources correctly.

To get density I multiplied the abundance estimate for each station by the predicted availability and divided by the area of the point count (based on Chandler et al. 2011).  I then took the mean across point counts within a stand and year to get density at the stand/year level.  And then used the quantiles from the bootstrap output to get the confidence intervals.

Does anyone see any problems with this approach?  Perhaps I should be using only ranef and the plots with bird data?  Am I accounting for enough variability using this bootstrap procedure?

Here's an example model and my preliminary script for getting the abundance estimate and the bootstrap confidence interval.  Also a few lines of the output.  I really appreciate any thoughts on this.

Best,

Mike Worland
Wisconsin DNR

(mod<-
global<- gmultmix(~block +year +cnpyCV +ba +scDiv +dbh +con +yb,
                             ~block +year +dayDiff,
                             ~obsvr +sky +windy +time +date +ba +sap, uf))
#
# Bootstrap function. Uses "predict" to estimate abundance for non-surveyed plots
# that have only habitat data; uses "ranef" to estimate abundance for plots that
# have both bird and habitat data. Also uses predict to estimate availability (phi).
# Abundance needs to be multiplied by availability & divided by area to calculate
# density.
#
Nhat <- function(mod) {
  ab <-bup(ranef(mod))
  ab<- cbind(ab,xplot[,c(1,2,4,10)])
  phi <-predict (mod, xplot, type ="phi", append=T)
  abNB<- predict(mod, habNB, type="lambda", append=T)
  phiNB <-predict (mod, habNB, type ="phi", append=T)
  names(ab)[names(ab) =="ab"] <-"abund"
  names(phi)[names(phi) =="Predicted"] <-"phi"
  names(phiNB)[names(phiNB) =="Predicted"] <-"phi"
  names(abNB)[names(abNB) =="Predicted"] <-"abund"
  mrgNB<-merge (phiNB[,c(1,5,32)],abNB[,c(1,5,29,32)], by=c("plot","year"),
              all.x=T,all.y=T)
  mrg<-merge (phi[,c(1,6,14)],ab[,c(1,3:5)], by=c("plot","year"),
              all.x=T,all.y=T)
  rb <-rbind (mrgNB,mrg)
  rb$dens <- (rb$abund*rb$phi)/0.07854
  ta<-tapply(rb$dens,list(rb$year,rb$stand),mean)
  ta<-data.frame(ta)
  x <-unlist(ta, use.names = F)
}
#
set.seed(1)
(pbN <- parboot(mod, Nhat, nsim=7, report=1)) #use nsim=200 for a "real" run

messages.body_plain:
hi Mike,
 in principle I think what you're doing is ok but one thing: Ranef() is not doing a bootstrap. Rather, it is computing the posterior mean and intervals by plugging in the MLE (so it is empirical Bayesian ).
 I guess it does make sense to bootstrap that, as you've done, to account for uncertainty due to having to estimate the parameters, but that is not related to the empirical Bayesianism of the whole thing.

regards
andy

Dear Joanna,

Generally, I would use similar rules of thumb as for regression modeling (e.g., 5-20 data points per parameter), but:

-          Remember that there are two n's in hierarchical models as say a site-occ model: one for sites and one for observations. Hence, you have much more information to estimate covariates that act on p than covariates that act on psi

-          You should perhaps have more sites per parameter for site-specific covariates in psi than according to any regression rules (e.g., 5-20 or whatever you choose), because you are estimating a regression on these covariates of an on- or only partially observed thing: the true presence/absence

One of the best ways of answering the "how many" questions such as yours is always to use simulation: simulate data sets of different size, analyse them with different numbers of covariates and save the estimates. Repeat for 1000 times and see how things vary as a function of sample size etc.

Kind regards  --- Marc

Imagine a candidate set of models: null (dot) models at one end (no temporal/spatial variation in anything), and fully time-dependent models at the other (imagine a t subscript for anything looking vaguely lke some Greek-letter-cum-parameter).  In the middle, you have some models where the variation over space or time is constrained to be a function of one or more 'covariates of interest'.

Given this 'continuum', then you could make the following rather dry observations:

1\ if the null model is the 'best' by various criterion, then your data are too sparse (or insufficient wrt model structure) to make any sort of interesting inference. A null model has no biological meaning, since there is no parameter outside of physics which is truly a constant over space time. So, a null model doesn't mean 'no temporal variation', it means 'your data set is insufficient to detect the variation that must be there, at least to some degree'.

2\ if the general model comes out on top, relative to your covariate models, then this is a different sort of problem. A fully general model indicates heterogeneity over time or space (or both), but, variation that isn't explained is meaningless white noise (and yes, even if you're estimating process variance for a PVA or some such, simply unexplained variation around a mean is a pretty naive estimator for process variance). Temporal or spatial variation in and of itself is *not* interesting. What *is* interesting is what 'drives' the variation. In most ecology, the drive-response sequence is 'inferred'. Meaning, unless we do an experiment, we're left with what JD Nichols calls 'post hoc story telling'. At the least, though, we can strive to tell interesting stories. So, if your general model wins, and does better than your covariate-constrained models (each of which is in effect 'a story'), then all you can conclude is that you're not a good story teller. More 'gently', it implies that your covariate set aren't particularly informative.

So, if you have a some degree of lack of resolution among the 'general' model and the 'covariate' models, then you have litytle basis for infering tat the covariates do much of anything. The fact that your general model does better than the null model means your data are at least sufficient to support that distinction. But failing to differentiate the general and covariate models is less a 'data' problem (at least, not directly), but is more a problem in terms of thinking hard about meaningful covariates. So, in response to Andy, I would submit that this is a 'problem', at least to some extent -- if the intent is to tell good stories. If the intent is driven by estimator parsimony, then if you average over the models, it won't make a lot of difference.

As for the whole delta AIC <4  or 2, or any of those sorts of rules of thumb, I would argue they're not particularly useful. If you're working with likelihood-based methods, then far better to use evidence ratios. You might want to have a look at section 4.4.1 in chapter 4 of the MARK book (marked or unmarked, the principles are the same): http://www.phidot.org/software/mark/docs/book/pdf/chap4.pdf

The general model (as understood by the *many* people who use that phrase -- some of them named Burnham, and Anderson, and so on) is the most parameterized model in the candidate model set. Since all parameters vary over space and time, then the usual starting point is to have a general model with time/space dependence in those parameters. if the data set is insufficient to fit to that model, then the general model is occasional a reduced parameter for of same, at least for some parameters. The assumption is that the general model adequately fits the data. Fit of all other models is scaled relative to that. Thats fundamental to GOF testing (where the general model is an approximation to a saturated model, which can't be specified for most data types), multi-model inference, and any number of things.

So, the distinction (which you could argue is semantic, although most of the estimation world refers to the most parameterized model as 'the general model') is made because it represents a point on the continuum for the candidate model set. Because it is general, it will fit, but have no explanatory power. That power comes from the comparison of other reduced models to the general model. if your gneral model is the best fitting, then you eally don't know anything other than the fact that you have 'variation', which is not particular informative (since variation at some level is a give).

Evan, to be clear I'm not questioning your expertise on this subject.  In the words of Wayne and Garth: "We're not worthy!"  To some extent I'm playing devil's advocate precisely because of the semantics.  And for this discussion to be useful to others, particularly the users of unmarked, sometimes things need to be described in the fullest detail.

So we've got a general model, a global model, and a saturated model.  FWIW, Burnham & Anderson (2002) mention them all but have an index entry only for "global model".  It is true they are all the same thing, conditional on a candidate model set - simply, the most parameterized model.  But unconditionally, the definitions of most parameterized model can differ, namely in that folks may disagree on what qualifies as most parameterized.  This was largely my point.

Theoretically, the most parameterized model contains a parameter for every single data point.  By every data point I mean the product of replicates across all sampled dimensions (e.g., for simple occupancy: sites*surveys).  This model fits perfectly but has no explanatory power.  Realistically, it cannot actually be fit for many model structures, particularly latent variable models.  Evan, you said that if the data set is insufficient, the general model is occasionally a reduced parameter model.  I would argue that, for applications relevant to unmarked and often elsewhere, it is ALWAYS a reduced parameter model.  B&A talk about selecting the global model to represent the most reasonably complex parameterization, which is different than being the theoretically most parameterized.

Therefore, if the theoretically most parameterized model is never actually the general model in a candidate set, then it is confusing to say that the general model has no explanatory power (at least in practice).  This is why I don't think having the general/global/saturated model as your best model is ever a problem.  Evan, you explained why Auriel may have received the concerns that she did.  I just wanted to further clarify why such concerns are not generally applicable to unmarked users.

My dear Brian,

to be honest, your post deserves the classic "RTFM" answer ! For instance, if you go to the example at the bottom of the help text of occuRN, you find this:
  ## Not run:

     data(birds)
     woodthrushUMF <- unmarkedFrameOccu(woodthrush.bin)
     # survey occasion-specific detection probabilities
     (fm.wood.rn <- occuRN(~ obsNum ~ 1, woodthrushUMF))

     # Empirical Bayes estimates of abundance at each site
     re <- ranef(fm.wood.rn)
     plot(re)
     ## End(Not run)

The more polite answer hence is: use ranef(). But only for occuRN and pcount, since only they model abundance, while occu() models presence/absence and therefore, ranef() gives you the estimate of the presence/absence state at each site. I get the impression that the following article is a obligate read:

Dorazio, R.M. 2007. On the choice of statistical models for estimating occurrence and extinction from animal surveys. Ecology 88: 2773--2782.

If you want the expected occurrence or abundance state (i.e., psi in the occupancy model and lambda in the two abundance models), you can use predict().

Kind regards  --  Marc

Generally, I would use similar rules of thumb as for regression modeling (e.g., 5-20 data points per parameter), but:

messages.body_plain:
Hi Russ,

There is no closed form of the posterior, but you can compute it using the forward or backward algorithms that are commonly used in the analysis of hidden Markov models. I implemented the backward algorithm following the approached outlined in one of the appendices of the original paper. Note that this involves summing over all possible value of N (up to K) for each site/primary-period, which takes a ton of time. MCMC can actually be faster when N is high.

Confidence intervals can be computed as quantiles of the posterior, which is demonstrated on the ranef help page. Source code is here:

https://github.com/rbchan/unmarked/blob/master/R/ranef.R

As is common in Empirical Bayes methods, the posterior distributions do not account for uncertainty about the hyperparameters (lambda, omega, gamma, etc...). I think you would have to adopt some sort of bootstrap to deal with that.

Richard

I did a general "ranef" search on the forum, but couldn't come up with an answer. Any suggestions/input is appreciated. Thanks!

Cheers,
Tim Schreckengost
Master's Candidate
Department of Entomology and Wildlife Ecology
University of Delaware

hi Tim,
 it's hard to say what's going on here.
 I think the scale of the random effects predictinos and the backtransformed linear predictor should be the same.
 I think your K is set too small here.  In addition it's possible that with a lot of over-dispersion the back-transformation of the linear predictor isn't giving very sensible point estimates and so may not be that meaningful.

 I'm just babbling here but I think in general you may not have a close correspondance between the exp(mu) and predictions of individual N's.
regards
andy

messages.body_plain:
Hi Diego,

There are 3 processes that you can model with pcountOpen: (1) spatial variation in initial abundance, (2) spatio-temporal variation in abundance after year 1, and (3) detection conditional on abundance. If you want to model the effect of habitat and whole on all years, then you need model both initial abundance using siteCovs and subsequent abundance using yearlySiteCovs. You only need obsCovs if you have robust design data.

Richard
